title: Lady Be Good
summary: B-24D Liberator Lady Be Good, a new aircraft with a first-time crew on their first combat mission, bombed Naples on April 4, 1943. On return, a sandstorm caused the crew to overshoot their air base at Soluch in Libya. The crew failed to realize they had overflown the base in the sandstorm and continued flying south into the Libyan Desert for many hours. When fuel was exhausted, eight of the nine crew members bailed out successfully. The survivors walked in the desert for eight days with only a single canteen of water to share, believing they were close to the Mediterranean coast. All nine crew members ultimately died.

Lady Be Good's crew were also new, having only arrived in Libya a week before on March 18, and they flew their first mission together on April 4.

A diary recovered from co-pilot Robert Toner indicated that none of the men were aware they had been flying over land when they bailed out, or that they were 400 miles inland. It has been speculated the dark empty desert floor may have resembled open sea.

title: United Airlines 521
summary: United Air Lines Flight 521, a Douglas DC-4 from LaGuardia Airport, failed to become airborne on 29 May 1947 while attempting takeoff on runway 18. The aircraft overran the end of the runway, ripped through the airport fence onto traffic on the Grand Central Parkway, and slammed into an embankment before plunging into a pond and exploding. Ten people escaped the flaming wreckage; only five survived. It was the worst commercial aviation disaster in United States history at the time.
probable_cause: The Civil Aeronautics Board determined the probable cause was either the failure of the pilot to release the gust lock before takeoff, or the decision to discontinue the takeoff because of apprehension resulting from rapid use of a short runway under calm wind conditions. Initial reports suggested wind shear may have been a factor, with a wind shift of almost unbelievable suddenness occurring during takeoff.

title: Pennsylvania Central Airlines 410
summary: Pennsylvania Central Airlines Flight 410, a Douglas DC-4, crashed into Lookout Rock in the West Virginia Blue Ridge Mountains at approximately 1,425 feet elevation while descending for Washington DC. All 50 passengers and crew were killed. The aircraft encountered thunderstorm weather, and the crew requested an alternate route requiring descent from 7,000 to 2,500 feet. The investigation found the pilot had erred in descending below the minimum altitude without adequate visual references and that ATC and the dispatcher provided an inappropriate clearance for an airway without established minimum altitude.

title: Pan Am 121
summary: A Lockheed L-049 Constellation suffered engine failure during cruise flight from Karachi to Istanbul, leading to overheating of remaining engines. One of the remaining engines then caught fire, which spread to the aircraft and caused structural damage. The burning magnesium parts separated from the aircraft, leaving it unable to maintain altitude, and it crashed in the Syrian desert at 4 miles from Mayadin. Fifteen people were killed.
probable_cause: Engine failure in the number one engine due to exhaust rocker arm fault. The crew elected to continue to Istanbul rather than divert to nearby airfields, causing the remaining engines to overheat. A subsequent engine fire spread to the aircraft structure, causing loss of altitude capability.

title: Dakota VT-CLA

The P-40s destroyed the left engine, causing the aircraft to dive and crash into a tree and paddy field, with all but one occupant killed.

title: BSAA Star Dust accident
summary: Star Dust, an Avro Lancastrian on charter from Buenos Aires to Santiago, crashed into Mount Tupungato at 15,000 feet after penetrating the poorly understood jet stream. The crew, believing they had cleared the mountain range at 24,000 feet and monitoring their calculated ground speed as exceeding their actual speed due to a headwind, descended into cloud-covered peaks they could not see. The aircraft hit the mountain at cruising speed with undercarriage retracted, indicating controlled flight into terrain. The wreckage was not found for 51 years, emerging from the Tupungato Glacier.
probable_cause: The accident resulted from controlled flight into terrain caused by navigational error. The crew mistakenly believed they had already cleared the Andes mountains and commenced descent when they were still a considerable distance to the east-northeast. This navigational error was likely caused by the crew's unfamiliarity with the jet stream, which produced an unexpected headwind that reduced their ground speed below their calculated assumptions, making them believe they were further west than they actually were.

factors.evidence: The aircraft crashed into Mount Tupungato at approximately 15,000 feet altitude, striking the mountain while in controlled flight with engines running near cruising speed and undercarriage retracted.

The crew mistakenly assumed their ground speed to be faster than it really was and deduced that they had already safely crossed the Andes, whereas they were still a considerable distance to the east-northeast and approaching the cloud-enshrouded Tupungato Glacier at high speed.
In the absence of visual sightings of the ground due to heavy clouds, the crew did not maintain awareness of their actual position relative to terrain.
Heavy clouds blocked visibility of the ground during the final portion of Star Dust's flight, preventing visual confirmation of position or terrain avoidance.
The jet stream phenomenon was not well understood in 1947, and the aircraft's navigation systems did not account for wind direction changes with altitude that the crew could not observe.

events.text: Aircraft cruising at 24,000 feet to cross Andes mountain range between Buenos Aires and Santiago.
Aircraft entered jet stream zone with headwind component, reducing actual ground speed significantly below crew's calculated assumptions.
Crew, mistakenly believing they had already cleared the mountain peaks, began descent toward Santiago.
Aircraft descended into cloud layers obscuring the cloud-covered Tupungato Glacier ahead, with no visual references available.

Aircraft impacted Mount Tupungato at high speed while in controlled flight, burying itself in snow and ice; the last Morse code transmission STENDEC was received by Santiago airport control tower four minutes before planned landing.

notes: Wreckage discovered in 1998 and 2000 in Tupungato Glacier at 15,000 feet elevation after 51+ years; previously missing.
The final Morse code transmission STENDEC has never been satisfactorily explained and remains a historical mystery.
Crew included experienced former RAF pilots; Captain Reginald Cook had DSO and DFC from WWII service.
Jet stream phenomenon not well understood in 1947, contributing to navigational assumptions.

title: United Air Lines 608
summary: In-flight fire in the baggage compartment developed from overfilled fuel tank venting into the cabin heater system. As the aircraft descended toward Bryce Canyon Airport, pieces of the aircraft including the right wing fell off. The crew was unable to maintain control in canyon gusts despite being only 10 feet above ground, and the aircraft crashed on National Park Service land. The fire and structural damage resulted from a design flaw in the cabin heater intake scoop placement relative to the fuel tank vent.
probable_cause: Design flaw: a cabin heater intake scoop was positioned too close to the number 3 alternate fuel tank air vent. When the fuel tank was overfilled during routine transfer, excess fuel was sucked into the cabin heater system and ignited. Contributing factors were inadequate crew training about the danger and failure to halt the fuel transfer before tank overflow.

title: General Leclerc's aviation accident
summary: A B-25 Mitchell transport aircraft carrying General Leclerc and 12 others departed Villacoublay for North Africa and crashed near Colomb-Béchar in bad weather conditions with sandstorms and strong headwinds. The aircraft had been modified by the French Air Force with an internal bunk at the rear, creating weight and balance issues. Investigation concluded the crash resulted from the aircraft being at too low an airspeed in the poor weather conditions, with passengers moving toward the rear of the aircraft inducing a flat spin.
probable_cause: The official report concluded the crash was due to recklessness of pilot François Delluc and persistence of General Leclerc in ignoring unfavorable weather conditions. title: BSAA Star Tiger disappearance
summary: BSAA Star Tiger, an Avro Tudor IV aircraft, disappeared without trace over the Atlantic Ocean on 30 January 1948 while en route from Santa Maria in the Azores to Bermuda. The aircraft was in radio contact until approximately 03:15 UTC when radio contact was lost. The investigation found want of care and attention to detail in the flight plan and noted the altitude chosen was much lower than usual. All 31 persons aboard disappeared.

title: 1948 Gatow air disaster
summary: A BEA Vickers Viking airliner on approach to RAF Gatow in West Berlin was struck by a Soviet Yakovlev Yak-3 fighter aircraft. The Soviet fighter was conducting aerobatic maneuvers in the vicinity of Gatow and had not coordinated with air traffic control. As the Viking made a left-hand turn on approach, the Yak-3 dived beneath it and pulled up sharply, clipping the Viking's port wing with its starboard wing. Both aircraft crashed; all occupants of both aircraft were killed. The incident occurred during escalating Cold War tensions over Berlin.
probable_cause: Midair collision caused by Soviet fighter aircraft conducting uncoordinated aerobatics in controlled airspace. The Yak-3 pilot was not under ATC control and failed to avoid the Viking on approach. Soviet aircraft were buzzing American and British passenger aircraft during this period of heightened tensions.

title: 1955 MacArthur Airport United Airlines crash
summary: On April 4, 1955, a Douglas DC-6 named Mainliner Idaho was conducting an instrument rating check when it crashed shortly after taking off from Long Island MacArthur Airport. Shortly after takeoff and only seconds after climbing through 150 ft, the plane began banking to the right. It continued to roll through 90 degrees; the nose then dropped suddenly and moments later it struck the ground. All three members of the flight crew were killed upon impact. During a simulated engine failure procedure, the check pilot had pulled the throttle lever for engine No. 4 past the idle position, reversing the propellers of that engine. When full power was applied to the reversed engine, it produced reverse thrust instead of forward thrust, causing an uncontrollable spiral dive.
probable_cause: One of the flight crew applied full power to No. 4 engine thinking this would bring the aircraft out of the increasing bank, but because the propellers were reversed and the flag was not raised, that increased the reverse thrust from No. 4 engine, causing the DC-6 to spiral out of control.

events.text: On April 4, 1955 at about 15:50 Eastern Standard Time, a United Air Lines check captain was carrying out instrument rating checks on two pilots using the Douglas DC-6 Mainliner Idaho.

Upon climbing through 50 ft, the aircraft began banking to the right at a rate which alarmed witnesses.

At a height of around 150 ft with all four engines producing take-off thrust, the nose began to fall and moments later the right wing and nose impacted the ground causing the fuselage to cartwheel over.
It was immediately engulfed in flames and all three members of the flight crew were instantly killed.

The CAB investigation identified three possible contributing factors: inaccurate altimeter reading, cloud obscuration of the mountain peak, or downdrafts around the peak.

title: 1956 Hawker Hunter multiple aircraft accident
summary: Eight RAF Hawker Hunter F.1 jet fighters from the Day Fighter Leader Squadron conducting a 4x4 dogfight exercise at 45,000 feet departed RAF West Raynham on February 8, 1956. By 11:00 a.m., weather at the home airfield had deteriorated with poor visibility, and the formation was diverted to nearby RAF Marham for a visual approach. Visibility suddenly reduced to near zero during approach with only 10 minutes of fuel remaining. Six of the eight aircraft were lost when pilots descended trying to locate the ground. Engines flamed out from fuel exhaustion as the aircraft descended below safe altitudes, and pilots ejected. One pilot (WW635) was killed when his aircraft crashed. The Board of Inquiry determined that sudden weather deterioration was the primary cause and the diversion to Marham on assumption of visual landing was an error of judgment.

All 22 of 36 occupants died.

title: Northwest Orient Airlines 2
summary: Northwest Airlines Flight 2, a Boeing 377 Stratocruiser, departed Seattle-Tacoma on April 2, 1956. Shortly after takeoff, the first officer retracted the wing flaps and the aircraft suddenly began to buffet violently and roll left. The captain, believing an asymmetric wing flap condition had developed, found the aircraft uncontrollable and decided to ditch in Puget Sound. All 40 occupants initially survived the ditching, but four passengers and one flight attendant died from hypothermia in the 42-degree water before rescue. Investigation revealed the flight engineer had failed to close the engine cowl flaps for takeoff.

summary: A TWA Constellation and United DC-7 collided over the Grand Canyon at 10:32 am in uncontrolled airspace. title: Braathens SAFE 253
summary: The de Havilland Heron crashed into Hummelfjell mountain at 1,350 meters altitude in Norway on 7 November 1956 at 9:50 while descending with icing and a downdraft. The aircraft was en route from Trondheim to Oslo when it began experiencing rapid atmospheric icing around Røros which exceeded the capacity of the ice protection system. Combined with a downdraft, the aircraft lost sufficient lift to remain airborne. The pilots turned the aircraft around to return to Trondheim, but the icing accumulated so rapidly that the aircraft lost altitude very quickly. Ice covered the windshield and radio antenna, disabling radio communication and navigation. The crew was unaware they were flying over the mountain when the aircraft struck terrain at 300 km/h, traveling tail-first.

title: Northwest Orient Airlines 710
summary: Northwest Airlines Flight 710, a Lockheed L-188 Electra flying from Chicago to Miami, broke up in midair over southern Indiana on March 17, 1960, after unexpectedly encountering clear-air turbulence at 18,000 ft; the right wing and part of the left wing separated and the aircraft plunged into farmland near Cannelton at over 600 mph, killing all 63 aboard. Investigators found the breakup closely resembled the 1959 Braniff Electra crash near Buffalo, Texas, and traced the cause to 'whirl mode' wing flutter: when an Electra's outboard engine mounting structure was damaged, high speed or turbulence could destroy the wing. The FAA restricted Electra operations and ordered Lockheed to redesign the structure.

Around the same time, U.S. Air Force B-57s operating nearby reported moderate to severe clear-air turbulence at high altitude, with one descending from 20,000-25,000 ft to 15,000 ft to escape it.

At about 3:20 p.m., in level flight at 400 mph, the aircraft's right wing separated from the fuselage, followed over six to ten seconds by the rest of the right wing and its engines; the outer left wing and its engine also broke away.

With its wings gone, the aircraft's momentum carried it more than 3 mi before it arced toward the ground, with an engine on the remaining left wing continuing to run at full power and accelerating the dive.
The aircraft struck farmland about 8 mi east of Cannelton, Indiana, nose-first at over 600 mph, leaving a crater about 15 ft deep and 30 ft wide.

summary: Viasa Flight 742, a McDonnell Douglas DC-9-32 registered YV-C-AVD, was on the Maracaibo-to-Miami leg of a flight from Caracas when it began its takeoff roll at 12:00 on 16 March 1969. Heading toward the Ziruma district, the aircraft failed to gain altitude and its left engine struck a power pole; as the plane banked left a reflector struck the fuel tank, spilling fuel, and after hitting a second power pole the left wing was ripped off and the left engine exploded into flames before the plane crashed in La Trinidad, Maracaibo. All 84 people aboard and 71 more on the ground were killed. Investigators attributed the crash to faulty sensors along with runway and takeoff calculations made from erroneous information, which left the aircraft overloaded by more than 5,000 pounds for the prevailing conditions.

title: 1969 Aswan Ilyushin Il-18 crash
summary: An Ilyushin Il-18 operated by United Arab Airlines, carrying Hajj pilgrims from Jeddah to Aswan, made two unsuccessful landing attempts in darkness with visibility reduced to 2-3 kilometers by a sandstorm on 20 March 1969. On a third approach the aircraft banked right and hit the left side of the runway, tearing off the starboard wing; the resulting fuel spillage caused the wreckage to burst into flames, killing 100 of the 105 aboard. Investigators found the pilot had descended below the minimum safe altitude without the runway lights clearly in sight, and cited fatigue from continuous working hours without suitable rest as a contributory factor.

title: TWA 5787
summary: Trans World Airlines Flight 5787, a Boeing 707 on a non-revenue proficiency training flight, crashed at Atlantic City on July 26, 1969, killing all five crew on board. The aircraft was conducting recurrent training and proficiency checks including simulated single-engine failure during takeoff and landing. After landing on runway 13, the crew requested immediate turnaround and go-around on runway 31. During the go-around briefed as a three-engine ILS approach with simulated engine 4 failure, the flight engineer called for flaps 25 and gear up at decision height. However, neither flaps nor landing gear moved. Approximately 16-18 seconds after the go-around call, the crew commented that all hydraulic power had been lost due to fatigue failure in the left outboard spoiler actuator. With low airspeed, three engines, and no hydraulics for rudder control, directional control was lost, the aircraft rolled and pitched down, and impacted the ground.
probable_cause: Loss of hydraulic power to the rudder in a critical flight condition combined with poor procedures for simulating engine failures and failure to apply correct hydraulic loss procedures; loss of directional control was unrecoverable.

With low airspeed, three engines, undercarriage down, full flaps, and no hydraulic rudder power, aircraft was incapable of recovery; rolled and pitched down impacting ground.

title: Aeroflot 826
summary: Aeroflot Flight N-826, an Antonov An-24B, crashed on 3 August 1969 during climb to 4200 meters near Preobrazhenka, Ukraine. title: Allegheny Airlines 853
summary: Allegheny Airlines Flight 853, a McDonnell Douglas DC-9, collided mid-air with a privately owned Piper PA-28 near Fairland, Indiana, on September 9, 1969. The DC-9 was on an instrument flight plan descending for approach to Indianapolis at 3,550 feet when it converged with the VFR Piper aircraft at a relative speed of 350 mph. The left wing of the PA-28 sheared off the DC-9's rear tail assembly. Both aircraft lost control and crashed, killing all 83 occupants on both aircraft. The collision resulted from deficiencies in air traffic control radar capabilities, the see-and-avoid concept under mixed IFR/VFR conditions, and the absence of regulations providing adequate separation of mixed traffic in terminal areas.
probable_cause: The deficiencies in the collision avoidance capability of the Air Traffic Control system in a terminal area with mixed IFR and VFR traffic. The deficiencies included inadequacy of the see-and-avoid concept, technical limitations of radar in detecting all aircraft, and absence of Federal Aviation Regulations providing adequate separation of mixed traffic.

The FAA system lacked adequate regulations for separating mixed IFR and VFR traffic in terminal areas.
The report faulted military and civilian aviation authorities for not reducing well-known collision risks that had existed for over a year.

title: 1970 Spantax Convair crash
summary: A Convair 990 Coronado operated by Spantax crashed shortly after takeoff from Stockholm Arlanda Airport on January 5, 1970, killing five of ten occupants. The aircraft was conducting a three-engine ferry flight after engine number 4 developed a fault. title: 1971 January 22 Surgut Aeroflot Antonov An-12 crash
summary: An Aeroflot Antonov An-12B departed Omsk Tsentralny Airport on 22 January 1971 bound for Surgut, carrying two flight crews, an engineer, loadmaster, and cargo. Upon descent toward Surgut, severe icing conditions were encountered at 400 to 1300 meters altitude. The aircraft's ice protection system was ineffective because engine bleed air valves were closed during the flight. As the aircraft descended to 1200 meters, ice accumulated on the wings, causing flow separation and a sudden loss of control. The aircraft entered an uncontrolled roll and crashed 15 kilometers short of the Surgut runway.

title: Aeroflot 1969
summary: Aeroflot Flight 1969, an Antonov An-10, crashed during approach to Luhansk on 31 March 1971. Shortly after receiving clearance to descend to 600 meters, approximately 13 square meters of the right wing including the aileron separated from the aircraft. The detached section struck the right horizontal stabilizer and elevator. The aircraft entered a steep bank and spiral dive, impacting the ground in a 60 degree pitch down attitude.

title: Aviogenex 130
summary: Aviogenex Flight 130, an international charter from Gatwick to Rijeka, took off at 16:33 GMT and suffered structural failure during landing on 23 May 1971. The Tupolev Tu-134A flipped over and caught fire. Investigation found that the crew might have suffered an optical illusion due to heavy showers and dusk that could have led them to believe the runway was closer and lower than it actually was. The crew executed an overly steep and fast descent in the last phase of final approach, causing a hard touchdown and breakage of the right wing, killing 78 out of 83 people.
probable_cause: Optical illusion caused by dusk, rain and water on runway led the crew to believe they were closer and higher from the runway than actually the case. The crew made a sharp nose-down input and reduced power to idle in the final phase, causing the aircraft to reach excessive speed and contact the runway with forces that broke the right wing.

title: TWA 742
summary: On 28 August 1973, TWA Flight 742, a Boeing 707 en route from Honolulu to Los Angeles during descent to FL110, experienced severe pitch oscillations over the Pacific Ocean. The aircraft underwent 50 abrupt pitch-up and pitch-down cycles in approximately 2 minutes, generating 2.4g peak acceleration forces. Investigation discovered that the left elevator had excessive waviness (0.42 inches) and was misaligned relative to the right, requiring different control forces. Unaware the aircraft was out of trim, the crew's descent control inputs triggered a classic pilot-induced oscillation. Two crew members and three passengers were injured; one critically injured passenger died two days later of intracranial bleeding.
probable_cause: Excessive waviness and misalignment of the left elevator relative to the right, combined with out-of-trim condition undetected by the crew, caused pilot-induced oscillation during descent when crew over-corrected control inputs attempting to level the aircraft.

factors.evidence: The upper skin of both elevators experienced waviness due to compression, with wave amplitude excessive: 0.42 inches for the left elevator and 0.32 for the right, and the left elevator deflected significantly further than the right with the same control column deflection.
With no one realizing it, when the accident 707 was expected to be properly trimmed, it was in fact flying slightly out of trim.

The crew used the amount of force and forward deflection of the control column that they were accustomed to on other 707s; on this particular aircraft, this amount of force was too great and deflected the elevator much more than the crew intended, pushing the aircraft into a violent downward pitch. Trying to rectify that, they pulled the yokes back, over-corrected, and caused yet another violent pitch-up instead of leveling off.
The 707 entered a violent porpoising motion, alternating abrupt pitch-up and pitch-down movement with 50 oscillations in about 2 minutes and peak acceleration forces of 2.4g.

events.text: Crew cleared to descend to FL 110; pilots disconnected the autopilot, reduced power and entered a descent from FL330.
As the 707 descended through 22,000 feet at 350 knots indicated airspeed, the nose abruptly pitched up; out-of-trim condition caused by excessive elevator waviness triggered pitch excursion.

Crew tried to level the aircraft but nose rapidly pitched down; pilots reduced engine power to idle, disengaged rudder power, Mach trim and yaw damper; aircraft entered violent porpoising with 50 oscillations in 2 minutes, 2.4g peak acceleration.
Oscillations gradually abated; crew regained level flight at 19,500 feet and continued descent to Los Angeles.

title: 1981 Pushkin Tu-104 crash

summary: A Boeing 747SP lost thrust in the No. 4 engine at 41,000 feet cruising over the Pacific. The autopilot slowly applied more aileron to keep the wings level until the maximum limit of 23 degrees was reached. As the speed decreased further, the aircraft began to roll to the right even though the autopilot was maintaining maximum left roll input.

By the time the captain disconnected the autopilot the aircraft had rolled over and plunged 31500 ft, experiencing high speeds and g-forces as high as 5 g before the captain was able to recover from the dive.

summary: Bar Harbor Airlines Flight 1808, a Beechcraft Model 99, departed Logan International Airport in Boston for Bangor, Maine, with planned stops in Augusta and Waterville, including an unscheduled flag stop in Auburn/Lewiston. At 22:00 EDT, weather at Auburn consisted of a 300-foot obscured indefinite ceiling, 1-mile visibility, and light drizzle. A Portland controller advised the flight it was drifting east of the ILS approach course and instructed a heading of 340 degrees. The aircraft flew through the approach course, requiring a 60-degree right turn less than 1 nautical mile from the outer marker. The aircraft did not begin descent until after passing Lewiston, already above the glide slope, causing the crew to rush the descent and approach with a steep descent profile. The aircraft crashed into trees 4,007 feet from the runway end and 440 feet to the right of centerline. All eight people on board were killed.
probable_cause: The National Transportation Safety Board determined the accident was caused by the crew's continued attempt to stabilize an unstable approach rather than executing a missed approach. Contributing factors included a late and large course correction by the controller that the captain accepted, possible altimeter setting error, the crew descending below the applicable minimum descent altitude without the required visual references, and continued descent below the published glide slope during a night approach in low visibility.

title: Space Shuttle Challenger disaster
summary: Space Shuttle Challenger disintegrated 73 seconds after launch on January 28, 1986, when record-low ambient temperatures stiffened the O-ring seals in the right Solid Rocket Booster's aft joint. Hot pressurized gas leaked through the compromised joint, burning through the attachment strut to the external tank. The structural failure led to rotation of the SRB and aerodynamic forces that tore the orbiter apart at Mach 1.92 approximately 46,000 feet above the Atlantic Ocean, killing all seven crew members instantly.
probable_cause: The accident was caused by the failure of the O-ring seals in the aft joint of the right Solid Rocket Booster. Record-low temperatures on launch morning stiffened the O-ring material, reducing its ability to seal the joint. The compromised seals allowed hot pressurized gas to escape, which burned through the aft attachment strut and the external tank. This structural failure caused the SRB to rotate, creating aerodynamic forces that destroyed the orbiter at Mach 1.92.

Similar foam shedding had occurred during previous Space Shuttle launches, but the hazard was not adequately addressed by the certification process.

The design did not include adequate warning or detection systems to alert crews of O-ring failure or excessive joint rotation.

title: Scandinavian Airlines System 751
summary: Scandinavian Airlines Flight 751, an MD-81 departing Stockholm Arlanda Airport, encountered dual engine failure 76 and 78 seconds after takeoff at an altitude of 3,220 feet after clear ice accumulated on the wings' inner roots and broke off, being ingested into both engines. The ice deformed fan blades, causing compressor stalls and engine surges that led to both engine failures. The pilots executed a successful emergency landing in a field near Gottröra with no fatalities among the 129 occupants.
probable_cause: Clear ice had formed on the upper side of the wings before takeoff but was not detected. De-icing fluid was applied but the aircraft was not checked afterwards for remaining ice as required. Ice pieces broke off during takeoff and were ingested into both engines, causing compressor stalls, engine surges, and complete engine failure. Contributing factors included inadequate training on engine surge recovery and insufficient information to the crew about the automatic thrust restoration system.

There was no simulator or other training on the engine surging problem; they were not trained in restoring engine operation after repeated surges

An automatic system, ATR (automatic thrust restoration), had not been described to the flight crew by SAS; SAS took part in theme conferences addressing clear ice but ATR was not documented within SAS
Engine no. 1 surged 39 seconds after takeoff and both engines failed at 76 and 78 seconds respectively, leaving the aircraft with no thrust

title: China Airlines 358
summary: China Airlines Flight 358, a Boeing 747-200F freighter, reported problems with number 3 engine several minutes after takeoff from Taipei at 5000 feet. The crew requested a left turn to return to the airport but reported being unable to turn left moments later. The aircraft struck a hill near Wanli at 700 feet. Investigation revealed the number 3 engine and pylon had separated from the aircraft due to failure of pylon midspar fittings.

title: Air Inter 148

agencies.name: Bureau of Enquiry and Analysis for Civil Aviation Safety

summary: Air Inter Flight 148 crashed into Mont Sainte-Odile in the Vosges Mountains while approaching Strasbourg Airport. The pilots set the autopilot to Vertical Speed Mode instead of Flight Path Angle Mode, then entered a descent rate of 3300 feet per minute instead of the intended 3.3 degrees. The ambiguous autopilot display showed only two digits, masking the actual high descent rate. The aircraft lacked a ground proximity warning system that might have alerted the crew.

title: USAir 405
summary: USAir Flight 405, a Fokker F28, was attempting to take off from LaGuardia Airport in poor weather conditions on March 22, 1992. Due to inadequate ground de-icing procedures at LaGuardia and weather-related delays up to 35 minutes, a significant accumulation of ice formed on the wings and airframe. The flight crew was unaware of the extent of ice buildup. The aircraft lifted off but failed to gain altitude, flying only several meters above the ground. The aircraft veered off the runway and struck several obstructions before coming to rest in Flushing Bay. Of the 51 people on board, 27 were killed, including the captain and one cabin crew member.
probable_cause: Ice accumulated on the wings and airframe due to inadequate de-icing procedures and weather delays, increasing drag and reducing lift. The aircraft attempted rotation at too low an airspeed, preventing the achievement of flight. Insufficient deicing procedures at LaGuardia, compounded by the crew's unawareness of ice extent, contributed to the accident.

title: Copa Airlines 201
summary: A 12-year-old Boeing 737-200 experienced a faulty wiring harness in the Attitude Director Indicator system that caused intermittent false data. The pilots switched both ADI displays to receive data from the same faulty gyro, creating a feedback loop where the aircraft appeared to be banking left when it was actually rolling right. This led to an uncontrolled 80-degree right roll and a vertical dive at supersonic speed, causing structural breakup at 10,000 feet. The aircraft crashed into jungle 29 minutes after takeoff with all 47 aboard killed.
probable_cause: Loss of control in flight due to faulty ADI wiring that produced erroneous instrument indications and resulted in inappropriate pilot control inputs. Contributing factors included incomplete training on ADI failure recovery and the design of the ADI switchover system that allowed both displays to be fed by the same faulty instrument.

title: GP Express 861
summary: The Beechcraft 99 operating Flight 861 from Atlanta to Anniston became confused about its position and course during approach in fog and low-lying clouds. The crew, an inadequately trained captain and inexperienced first officer, experienced intercom and system problems that degraded communication. They attempted an approach from excessive altitude and airspeed without completing published procedures. The aircraft was on final approach when it entered a steep bank exceeding 60 degrees to align with the runway while airspeed decayed. At 200 feet above ground, the right wing stalled. The aircraft struck terrain 1,400 feet from the runway end. All three crew members survived with serious injuries.
probable_cause: Captain Chapo became fixated on locating an inoperative strobe light marking the Cuban border, causing him to begin the turn to final approach too late. This forced a steep bank to maintain alignment while airspeed decayed. Crew fatigue from 23.5 hours awake and circadian rhythm disruption contributed to impaired judgment, cognitive fixation, and poor communication about decreasing airspeed.

title: 1993 Tajik Air Yakovlev Yak-40 incident
summary: A Yakovlev Yak-40 crashed during takeoff at Khorog Airport when militants forced the crew to accept 81 passengers on an aircraft designed to carry only 28, exceeding maximum takeoff weight by 3,000 kg. Unable to become airborne, the aircraft overran the runway at high speed. The left main landing gear struck an earth embankment 148-150 meters beyond the runway end. The aircraft then struck a boulder and a concrete pillbox before falling into the Panj River and disintegrating. Four passengers survived.
probable_cause: Severe aircraft overloading caused by forced acceptance of excess passengers under threat during civil war, preventing takeoff and causing runway overrun with terrain strike.

title: China Airlines 605
summary: A China Airlines Boeing 747-400 went off the runway when attempting to land at Hong Kong's Kai Tak Airport on 4 November 1993 during Typhoon Ira with extreme crosswind conditions. The aircraft touched down 2,100 feet past the runway's displaced threshold at 150 knots and floated in strong winds. After overrunning the runway, the captain deliberately turned left to avoid approach lights, causing a ground loop that slid the aircraft into Victoria Harbour. All occupants survived. It was the first hull loss of a 747-400.
probable_cause: The captain failed to initiate the mandatory missed approach procedure when observing severe airspeed fluctuations, wind shear and glide slope deviation alerts. The first officer lacked sufficient experience to handle the aircraft in crosswind conditions, and the airline lacked clear crosswind landing procedures in their manuals.

title: Baikal Airlines 130
summary: Tu-154M experienced engine starter failure in No. 2 engine during startup with an alarming red light indication that warned of dangerous air start unit rotational speed. The flight crew ignored the warning, deemed it a false alarm based on aircraft design knowledge and flight manual guidance stating such alarms do not require immediate action. As thrust was set for takeoff, the starter mechanism rotated at dangerous speed, rupturing oil and hydraulic lines in the engine compartment. This ignited an uncontrollable fire and destroyed the aircraft's hydraulic systems causing loss of control in initial climb. The aircraft crashed into a dairy farm near Irkutsk killing all occupants.
probable_cause: Engine starter failed and broke apart, rupturing oil and hydraulic lines and igniting fire that destroyed the aircraft's hydraulic systems. Crew misidentified the red alarm as false based on design assumptions, inadequate training on alarm significance, and flight manual guidance that did not require immediate action for such alerts.

title: United Express 6291

The crew misinterpreted the decreasing oil pressure and degraded climb performance as engine failure, declared a Pan-Pan, and began an unstable descent.

title: Atlantic Southeast Airlines 529
summary: Atlantic Southeast Airlines Flight 529, an Embraer EMB 120 Brasilia, crashed on August 21, 1995, while climbing through 18,100 feet between Atlanta and Gulfport. Hamilton Standard and the FAA failed to require recurrent on-wing ultrasonic inspections.

title: Austral Líneas Aéreas 2553
summary: Austral Líneas Aéreas Flight 2553 crashed on the lands of Estancia Magallanes when ice formed inside the pitot tube during descent through a cumulonimbus cloud. The first officer deployed slats to maintain altitude despite the captain's order to reduce speed, causing asymmetric airflow that tore one slat from the aircraft. The aircraft became uncontrollable and crashed at a 70-degree nose-down attitude.

events.text: At 22:10 ADT while flying over Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, the flight crew detected an odour in the cockpit and determined it was smoke from the air conditioning system.
Four minutes later the odour returned and smoke became visible, prompting the pilots to make a pan-pan call to Moncton Centre and request a diversion.

Following the Swissair 'Smoke/fumes of unknown origin' checklist, the crew shut off power to the cabin using the CABIN BUS switch, which also turned off the recirculating fans and allowed the fire to spread toward the cockpit.
At 22:24:28 the crew reported 'we now must fly manually' as the fire cut power to the autopilot, then declared an emergency ten seconds later in the last transmission received from Flight 111.

In a smoke-filled cockpit with almost no flight instruments, First Officer Löw may have become spatially disoriented, and the aircraft struck the ocean near St. Margarets Bay at an estimated 345 mph at 22:31:18 ADT.

title: Wuhan Airlines 343
summary: Wuhan Airlines Flight 343, a Xian Y-7, crashed on 22 June 2000 while attempting to land at Wuhan Wangjiadun Airport during severe weather. The aircraft circled the airport for 30 minutes in thunderstorm conditions with 451 thunderclaps in 10 minutes. The crew debated diverting but the captain decided to continue the approach. The aircraft was struck by lightning and encountered windshear, becoming uncontrollable. The fuselage broke into two sections; all 38 passengers and 4 crew were killed, along with 7 people on the ground.
probable_cause: The aircraft was struck by lightning and encountered windshear while attempting to land during severe thunderstorm conditions. The crew and ATC both violated standard operating procedures for severe weather, and the captain made an incorrect decision to continue the approach rather than divert to an alternate airport.

The aircraft touched down on the runway at 300 kph without landing gear extended, skidded 650 m, then lifted off again. After 16 minutes airborne, the crew lowered the landing gear and landed safely.

title: Hapag-Lloyd 3378
summary: An Airbus A310 departed Chania with the landing gear unable to retract, leaving it in the fully extended position. The flight crew did not account for the extra drag caused by the extended gear when using the Flight Management System to estimate fuel consumption. After the captain diverted to Munich, then to Vienna when fuel reserves fell critically low, the aircraft ran out of fuel during the approach and crash-landed just short of runway 34. No fatalities resulted, but the aircraft was written off.
probable_cause: The crew failed to comply with company regulations regarding fuel reserves and relied exclusively on Flight Management System calculations without accounting for the increased fuel consumption caused by the extended landing gear.

factors.evidence: It was found to be impossible to fully retract the landing gear, as indicated by both the red 'gear unsafe' lamp and the yellow 'gear door open' lamp.

The investigation r[evealed] the cause of the failure of landing gear retraction as a minor oversight during maintenance; an inadequately secured lock nut allowed a screw to gradually turn, eventually leading to a 10 mm adjustment error that prevented complete retraction.
Airbus documentation failed to adequately and clearly inform flight crew of the limitations that apply to fuel management using the FMS.
Fuel reserves were determined exclusively using the FMS, due to lack of awareness of its inapplicability with gear down.
The crew had to cope with a heavier cockpit workload that was aggravated by the unavailability of the airline HF radio station for technical consultation.
The crew failed to comply with company regulations regarding fuel reserves, caused by several human factors, most importantly extreme work load and stress, leading to loss of situational awareness.

At 11:57CEST, the first officer noted and reported to the captain that they had already consumed half of their initial fuel load, although they had progressed to only their last waypoint still inside Greece. At 12:34CEST, the FMS prediction for fuel remaining upon arrival at Vienna fell to critically low.
The plane eventually ran out of fuel while attempting a diversion to Vienna, crash-landing just short of runway 34.

Investigation found the crew made high-pitch attitude maneuvers with engines at idle and elected to execute a go-around instead of stall recovery.

title: Air France 4590
summary: Air France Flight 4590 ran over debris on the runway dropped by a preceding Continental Airlines DC-10, causing a tyre to explode and disintegrate during takeoff at 185 mph. The aircraft lifted off but the loss of thrust, high drag from extended landing gear, and fire damage to flight controls made it impossible to maintain control. The Concorde crashed into a hotel in Gonesse two minutes after takeoff.

title: Gulf Air 072
summary: Gulf Air Flight 072, an Airbus A320-212 flying from Cairo to Bahrain, crashed into the shallow waters of the Persian Gulf 2 km from the airport on 23 August 2000, minutes after a go-around from a failed approach to Runway 12. The captain suffered spatial disorientation, applying a large nose-down input that produced a 15-degree dive; as the aircraft descended, the crew disregarded the GPWS 'sink rate' and 'Whoop, whoop, pull up' warnings while debating flap configuration instead. The Airbus struck the sea at 280 knots, killing all 143 people on board.

title: 2000 Australia Beechcraft King Air crash
summary: A chartered Beechcraft climbed to 34,300 feet above its cleared altitude of 25,000 feet. The autopilot maintained level flight on a north-easterly heading for five hours as the left engine exhausted fuel. The aircraft crashed 65 km southeast of Burketown with all eight occupants killed.

The aircraft continued flying on a straight north-easterly heading for five hours, before exhausting its fuel and crashing 65 km south-east of Burketown.

title: Aeroméxico 250
summary: The DC-9-31 overran the runway on landing at General Lucio Blanco International Airport in Reynosa during adverse weather caused by the remains of Hurricane Keith. All 88 people on board survived, but 64 were injured; four ground residents were killed.

title: Singapore Airlines 006
summary: During heavy rain from Typhoon Xangsane with poor visibility, the aircraft was cleared for takeoff but lined up on the closed runway 05R instead of the assigned runway 05L. The pilots did not see construction equipment on the closed runway and collided with excavators and other machinery after 41 seconds at full throttle. The aircraft broke apart and caught fire, destroying the forward fuselage section. The accident exposed systemic failures including the lack of ground radar, absence of physical barriers or hazard markings on the closed runway, and active taxiway lighting that guided pilots into the construction zone.

title: Dirgantara Air Service 3130
summary: The Britten-Norman Islander, carrying 18 people including the captain and 17 passengers, took off from Datah Dawai. title: British Airways 2069
summary: At cruise level 42,000 feet, a mentally unstable Kenyan passenger stormed the flight deck and attempted to seize control of the Boeing 747. First Officer Watson recovered the aircraft to level flight. Minor injuries occurred from violent pitch changes; the aircraft continued to Nairobi. The captain and crew were later honored for their actions.

title: ELK Airways 1007
summary: ELK Airways Flight 1007, an Antonov An-28, departed Tallinn Airport at around 18:05 local time for a short domestic flight to Kärdla on Hiiumaa island. Weather conditions included winds up to 44 km/h, visibility 8 km, cloud ceiling 370 m, temperature 0 degrees Celsius, and icing conditions highly possible. To avoid icing conditions present in the area, the crew switched from an instrument approach to a visual approach. However, the aircraft descended below the minimum decision altitude, entered clouds, and lost visual contact. At approximately 18:53 local time, the aircraft impacted treetops and crashed into a marshland about 1.5 km south-east of the airport runway. The marsh absorbed impact forces and prevented a post-crash fire. One passenger died on impact; a ten-year-old boy died in hospital on 29 November from his injuries. Total fatalities: two.

The crew decided to descend below the minimum decision altitude without obtaining visual contact with the runway.

title: Royal Air Force Nimrod XV230
summary: Royal Air Force Hawker Siddeley Nimrod XV230, the first Nimrod to enter service in 1969, suffered an in-flight fuel leak during mid-air refuelling while monitoring Operation Medusa. title: Agni Air 101
summary: Agni Air Flight 101 crashed 50 miles south of Kathmandu 25 minutes after takeoff when both generators failed, causing loss of flight instruments. title: UTair 120

title: Sepahan Airlines 5915

title: Southwest Airlines 3472

location.name: Gulf of Mexico, diverted to Pensacola

summary: Southwest Airlines Flight 3472, a Boeing 737-700, experienced an engine failure on August 27, 2016, at 31,000 feet over the Gulf of Mexico, 12 minutes after departure from New Orleans. The airport was not approved for Boeing 727-200 operations and the civil aviation authority had not enforced this regulation.

The aircraft descended out of control and broke up in mid-air, killing all thirteen occupants.

title: 2026 Mount Ololokwe helicopter crash
summary: A Eurocopter EC130 B4 helicopter operated by Lady Lori Helicopters crashed in rugged terrain in the foothills of Mount Ololokwe on August 19, 2026 on a charter flight from Loisaba Conservancy toward the Ewaso Ng'iro area. All seven occupants were killed including pilot Josh Outram, an experienced helicopter pilot with over 15 years flying experience in Kenya. The crash site lay in difficult terrain that hampered search and recovery efforts, with fire at the crash site impeding investigation. The Kenya Civil Aviation Authority launched an investigation but the cause was not immediately determined.
